# 2. Data cleaning


## 2.1 - 2.6 Blanks, missing values and duplicates

```{r cleaning-basic}
# 2.1 Create a working copy of the original dataset
books_clean <- books

# 2.2 Convert blank strings or whitespace-only strings to NA safely across character columns
character_cols <- names(books_clean)[sapply(books_clean, is.character)]

for (col in character_cols) {
  books_clean[[col]][!is.na(books_clean[[col]]) & trimws(books_clean[[col]]) == ""] <- NA
}

# 2.3 Check missing values after string-to-NA conversion
print(colSums(is.na(books_clean)))

# 2.4 Count exact duplicate observations
n_duplicates <- sum(duplicated(books_clean))
cat("Total duplicate rows found:", n_duplicates, "\n")

# 2.5 Remove exact duplicate observations (keeping the first occurrence)
books_clean <- books_clean[!duplicated(books_clean), , drop = FALSE]

# Reset row indices
rownames(books_clean) <- NULL

# 2.6 Verify cleaned dataset dimensions and zero duplicates
cat("Cleaned dataset dimensions:", dim(books_clean), "\n")
cat("Remaining duplicate rows:", sum(duplicated(books_clean)), "\n")
```

## 2.7 - 2.8 Weight conversion to kilograms

```{r weight-conversion}
# 2.7 Inspect weight column to find the units of measurement
# Extract measurement units from the weight column
weight_units <- gsub("[0-9\\.]", "", books_clean$weight)
weight_units <- trimws(weight_units)

# 2.8 Convert weight to kilograms
# Extract numeric portion of weight string
weight_numeric <- as.numeric(gsub("[^0-9\\.]", "", books_clean$weight))


books_clean$weight_kg <- ifelse(
  weight_units == "ounces",
  weight_numeric * 0.028349523125,
  ifelse(
    weight_units == "pounds",
    weight_numeric * 0.45359237,
    NA_real_
  )
)
#Inspect converted weight results
print(head(books_clean[, c("weight", "weight_kg")]))
print(summary(books_clean$weight_kg))
print(sum(!is.na(books_clean$weight_kg)))
```

## 2.9 - 2.20 Outliers, consistency checks, final dataset

```{r cleaning-outliers}
# 2.9 Investigate extreme weight values

# Display the 10 books with the lowest weights
print(
  head(
    books_clean[
      order(books_clean$weight_kg),
      c("price", "pages", "weight", "weight_kg")
    ],
    10
  )
)

# Display the 10 books with the highest weights
print(
  head(
    books_clean[
      order(books_clean$weight_kg, decreasing = TRUE),
      c("price", "pages", "weight", "weight_kg")
    ],
    10
  )
)


# 2.10 Detect weight outliers using the IQR method

# Calculate the first and third quartiles
Q1 <- quantile(books_clean$weight_kg, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)
Q3 <- quantile(books_clean$weight_kg, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)

# Calculate the interquartile range
IQR_weight <- Q3 - Q1

# Calculate the lower and upper bounds
lower_bound <- Q1 - 1.5 * IQR_weight
upper_bound <- Q3 + 1.5 * IQR_weight

# Display the calculated values
print("1st quartile:")
print(Q1)
print("3rd quartile:")
print(Q3)
print("IQR:")
print(IQR_weight)
print("Lower bound:")
print(lower_bound)
print("Upper bound:")
print(upper_bound)

# Identify weight outliers
weight_outliers <- books_clean[
  !is.na(books_clean$weight_kg) &
    (books_clean$weight_kg < lower_bound |
      books_clean$weight_kg > upper_bound),
]

# Count weight outliers
print(nrow(weight_outliers))

# Display detected outliers
print("Detected weight outliers:")
print(weight_outliers[, c(
  "price", "pages",
  "weight", "weight_kg"
)])


# 2.11 Investigate potentially implausible weights

# Calculate grams per page
books_clean$g_per_page <- (
  books_clean$weight_kg * 1000
) / books_clean$pages

# Display summary statistics
print(summary(books_clean$g_per_page))

# Exploratory thresholds for suspicious values
# These are diagnostic thresholds, not proven error limits
lower_gpp <- 0.3
upper_gpp <- 10

# Flag potentially suspicious observations
implausible_weight <- !is.na(books_clean$g_per_page) &
  (books_clean$g_per_page < lower_gpp |
    books_clean$g_per_page > upper_gpp)

# Count flagged observations
print(sum(implausible_weight))

# Inspect flagged observations
print(
  books_clean[
    implausible_weight,
    c(
      "price", "pages", "weight",
      "weight_kg", "g_per_page"
    )
  ]
)

# Keep the original weights until further investigation
# Do not automatically replace flagged values with NA
# Remove the temporary diagnostic variable
books_clean$g_per_page <- NULL

# Verify the dataset dimensions
print(dim(books_clean))


# 2.12 Detect outliers in other numeric variables (IQR method)

# Function that returns the number of IQR outliers of a variable
count_outliers <- function(x) {
  q1 <- quantile(x, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)
  q3 <- quantile(x, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
  iqr <- q3 - q1
  sum(x < q1 - 1.5 * iqr | x > q3 + 1.5 * iqr, na.rm = TRUE)
}

# Apply the function to the main numeric variables
outlier_vars <- c("price", "pages", "avg_reviews", "n_reviews", "weight_kg")
print(sapply(books_clean[, outlier_vars], count_outliers))


# 2.13 Consistency checks for review variables

star_vars <- c("star5", "star4", "star3", "star2", "star1")

# Books without reviews have undefined star proportions
books_clean[books_clean$n_reviews == 0, star_vars] <- NA

# Check star proportions only for books with reviews
reviewed_books <- books_clean$n_reviews > 0

star_sum <- rowSums(
  books_clean[reviewed_books, star_vars]
)

# Summary of star proportions
print(summary(star_sum))

# Count inconsistencies (tolerance: 0.05)
print(sum(abs(star_sum - 1) > 0.05, na.rm = TRUE))

# Check average rating range
print(range(books_clean$avg_reviews, na.rm = TRUE))

# Check invalid price and page values
print(sum(books_clean$price <= 0, na.rm = TRUE))
print(sum(books_clean$pages <= 0, na.rm = TRUE))

# Count books without reviews
print(sum(books_clean$n_reviews == 0))


# 2.14 Convert language to a factor
books_clean$language <- factor(books_clean$language)
print(table(books_clean$language, useNA = "ifany"))
# Almost all books are in English, so language is not useful
# for group comparisons.


# 2.15 Final check of the cleaned dataset
# Missing values are kept; na.rm = TRUE is used in the calculations
# so that no books are removed unnecessarily.
print(colSums(is.na(books_clean)))
str(books_clean)


# 2.16 Estimate typical grams per page

# Calculate grams per page
g_per_page <- books_clean$weight_kg * 1000 / books_clean$pages

# Flag potentially implausible values
suspicious_weight <- !is.na(g_per_page) &
  (g_per_page < 0.3 | g_per_page > 10)

# Use only observations with available, non-suspicious ratios
valid_gpp <- g_per_page[
  !is.na(g_per_page) & !suspicious_weight
]

# Calculate the mean and median
print(mean(valid_gpp))
print(median(valid_gpp))

# Check how much the values vary
print(sd(valid_gpp))
print(summary(valid_gpp))


# 2.17 Compare weight statistics with and without suspicious values

# Create a temporary copy of the weight variable
weight_without_suspicious <- books_clean$weight_kg

# Exclude suspicious weights from the comparison only
weight_without_suspicious[suspicious_weight] <- NA

# Compare descriptive statistics
comparison <- data.frame(
  Statistic = c("Mean", "Median", "SD"),
  Original = c(
    mean(books_clean$weight_kg, na.rm = TRUE),
    median(books_clean$weight_kg, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd(books_clean$weight_kg, na.rm = TRUE)
  ),
  Without_Suspicious = c(
    mean(weight_without_suspicious, na.rm = TRUE),
    median(weight_without_suspicious, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd(weight_without_suspicious, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
)

# Display the comparison
print(comparison)


# 2.18 Create a separate weight variable for analysis

# Preserve original weight measurements
books_clean$weight_analysis <- books_clean$weight_kg

# Mark suspicious measurements as missing for analysis
books_clean$weight_analysis[suspicious_weight] <- NA

# Check the number of excluded measurements
print(sum(is.na(books_clean$weight_analysis)))

# Compare available observations
print(sum(!is.na(books_clean$weight_kg)))
print(sum(!is.na(books_clean$weight_analysis)))


# 2.19 Compare correlations before and after excluding suspicious weights

# Correlation using original weight measurements
cor_original <- cor(
  books_clean$pages,
  books_clean$weight_kg,
  use = "complete.obs"
)

# Correlation excluding suspicious weight measurements
cor_filtered <- cor(
  books_clean$pages,
  books_clean$weight_analysis,
  use = "complete.obs"
)

# Display results
print(cor_original)
print(cor_filtered)


# 2.20 Final feature selection and export

# Remove language because it has very low variability
# The language distribution was already examined in Step 2.14
# Keep a copy of language for the categorical bar chart (Section 4.14)
language_for_plot <- books_clean$language
books_clean$language <- NULL

# Remove the original text weight variable
# The converted weight_kg variable is retained
books_clean$weight <- NULL

# Check final dimensions and variables
print(dim(books_clean))
print(names(books_clean))

books_export <- books_clean[, setdiff(names(books_clean), "weight")]
# Save the final cleaned dataset
write.csv(books_export,
         "data/Amazon_Data_Science_Books_final.csv",
          row.names = FALSE)
# Verify the exported dataset
books_check <- read.csv(
  "data/Amazon_Data_Science_Books_final.csv"
 )

print(dim(books_check))
print(names(books_check))
```

# 3. Summary statistics

```{r summary-statistics}
# 3.1 Select the numeric variables
# Use weight_analysis for the filtered weight summary

num_vars <- c(
  "price", "pages", "avg_reviews", "n_reviews",
  "star5", "star4", "star3", "star2", "star1",
  "weight_analysis"
)


# 3.2 Define a function to calculate skewness
# Positive: right-skewed distribution
# Negative: left-skewed distribution
# Close to zero: approximately symmetric

skewness <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]

  if (length(x) < 3 || sd(x) == 0) {
    return(NA_real_)
  }

  mean((x - mean(x))^3) / sd(x)^3
}


# 3.3 Define a function for descriptive statistics

describe <- function(x) {
  c(
    n = sum(!is.na(x)),
    missing = sum(is.na(x)),
    mean = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    variance = var(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    min = min(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    Q1 = unname(quantile(x, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)),
    Q3 = unname(quantile(x, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)),
    max = max(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    range = diff(range(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
    IQR = IQR(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    CV = sd(x, na.rm = TRUE) / mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    skewness = skewness(x)
  )
}


# 3.4 Create the descriptive statistics table

summary_table <- t(
  sapply(books_clean[, num_vars, drop = FALSE], describe)
)

print(round(summary_table, 3))
if (!dir.exists("plots")) {
  dir.create("plots", recursive = TRUE)
}
png("plots/3_4_weight_outliers.png",
    width = 8, height = 6,
    units = "in", res = 150)

boxplot(
  books_clean$weight_kg,
  main = "Outlier Detection in Book Weight",
  ylab = "Book Weight (kg)",
  col = "lightblue",
  border = "darkblue",
  pch = 16
)

dev.off()

# 3.5 Compare original and filtered weight statistics

weight_comparison <- rbind(
  weight_kg = describe(books_clean$weight_kg),
  weight_analysis = describe(books_clean$weight_analysis)
)

print(round(weight_comparison, 3))


# 3.6 Check missing values in the final dataset

print(colSums(is.na(books_clean)))


# 3.7 Verify the final dataset dimensions

print(dim(books_clean))

# Step 3.8 - Calculate Coefficient of Variation (%)

cv_percent <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  100 * sd(x) / mean(x)
}

sapply(
  books_clean[c("price", "pages", "avg_reviews",
                "n_reviews", "weight_analysis")],
  cv_percent
)
```

# 4. Data visualization

## 4.1 - 4.7 Base R plots

```{r visualization-base}
# Create a folder for the plots


# 4.1 Histograms of the main numeric variables

main_vars <- c(
  "price",
  "pages",
  "avg_reviews",
  "n_reviews",
  "weight_analysis"
)

png(
  "plots/4_1_histograms.png",
  width = 12,
  height = 8,
  units = "in",
  res = 150
)

# Arrange plots in 2 rows and 3 columns
par(
  mfrow = c(2, 3),
  cex.main = 1.3,
  cex.lab = 1.2,
  cex.axis = 1.0
)

# Create a histogram for each variable
for (v in main_vars) {
  hist(
    books_clean[[v]],
    main = paste("Histogram of", v),
    xlab = v,
    col = "lightblue",
    border = "white",
    breaks = 30
  )
}

# Reset graphical parameters
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# Save and close the image file
dev.off()


# Observations:
# - Price is right-skewed, with a few expensive books.
# - Pages is right-skewed, with some very large books.
# - Average ratings are left-skewed, with most ratings
#   concentrated between 4 and 5.
# - Number of reviews is extremely right-skewed.
# - Filtered weight is right-skewed, but extreme
#   suspicious measurements have been excluded.


# 4.2 Boxplots of the main numeric variables

png(
  "plots/4_2_boxplots.png",
  width = 12,
  height = 8,
  units = "in",
  res = 150
)

# Arrange plots in 2 rows and 3 columns
par(
  mfrow = c(2, 3),
  cex.main = 1.3,
  cex.lab = 1.2,
  cex.axis = 1.0
)

# Create a boxplot for each variable
for (v in main_vars) {
  boxplot(
    books_clean[[v]],
    main = paste("Boxplot of", v),
    ylab = v,
    col = "lightblue",
    border = "darkblue",
    pch = 16,
    cex = 0.6
  )
}

# Reset graphical parameters
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# Save and close the image file
dev.off()


# Observations:
# - Price contains several high-value outliers.
# - Pages contains books with unusually high page counts.
# - Average ratings contain some unusually low values.
# - Number of reviews has many extreme high values.
# - Filtered weight still contains some outliers.
# - Outliers are not automatically removed.


# 4.3 Histogram of log-transformed number of reviews

# Apply log(1 + x) to handle zero reviews
log_reviews <- log1p(books_clean$n_reviews)

# Save the histogram
png(
  "plots/4_3_log_reviews.png",
  width = 9,
  height = 6,
  units = "in",
  res = 150
)

hist(
  log_reviews,
  breaks = 30,
  main = "Histogram of Log-Transformed Reviews",
  xlab = "log(1 + Number of Reviews)",

  border = "white"
)

dev.off()


# Compare skewness before and after transformation
print(skewness(books_clean$n_reviews))
print(skewness(log_reviews))


# Observation:
# The logarithmic transformation reduces the influence
# of very large review counts and makes the distribution
# easier to visualize.
```

## 4.8 Variability, log transformations and correlation heatmap

```{r variability-correlation}
# Ensure the plots directory exists
if (!dir.exists("plots")) {
  dir.create("plots", recursive = TRUE)
}

# 1. Plotting the histograms for understanding the variability of the data
png("plots/histograms_grid.png", width = 10, height = 12, units = "in", res = 150)
par(mfrow = c(3, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1)) # Optimized margins to prevent margin errors

hist(books_clean$price, main = "Distribution of Price", xlab = "Price", col = "skyblue", border = "black")
hist(books_clean$pages, main = "Distribution of Pages", xlab = "Pages", col = "lightgreen", border = "black")
hist(books_clean$n_reviews, main = "Distribution of Reviews", xlab = "Number of Reviews", col = "pink", border = "black")
hist(books_clean$avg_reviews, main = "Distribution of Average Reviews", xlab = "Average Reviews", col = "yellow", border = "black")
hist(books_clean$weight_kg, main = "Distribution of Weight", xlab = "Weight (kg)", col = "grey", border = "black")

dev.off()
par(mfrow = c(1, 1)) # Reset layout


# 2. Create log-transformed columns (using + 1 to handle zeros safely)
books_clean$log_price     <- log(books_clean$price + 1)
books_clean$log_pages     <- log(books_clean$pages + 1)
books_clean$log_n_reviews <- log(books_clean$n_reviews + 1)
books_clean$log_weight    <- log(books_clean$weight_kg + 1)


# 3. Plot the original variables against avg_reviews
png("plots/scatterplots_original.png", width = 1600, height = 1200, res = 180)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))

plot(books_clean$price, books_clean$avg_reviews,
     xlab = "Price", ylab = "Avg Reviews",
     main = "Price vs Avg Reviews", col = "darkblue", pch = 16, cex = 0.6)

plot(books_clean$pages, books_clean$avg_reviews,
     xlab = "Pages", ylab = "Avg Reviews",
     main = "Pages vs Avg Reviews", col = "darkblue", pch = 16, cex = 0.6)

plot(books_clean$n_reviews, books_clean$avg_reviews,
     xlab = "Number of Reviews", ylab = "Avg Reviews",
     main = "N_Reviews vs Avg Reviews", col = "darkblue", pch = 16, cex = 0.6)

plot(books_clean$weight_kg, books_clean$avg_reviews,
     xlab = "Weight (kg)", ylab = "Avg Reviews",
     main = "Weight vs Avg Reviews", col = "darkblue", pch = 16, cex = 0.6)

dev.off()
par(mfrow = c(1, 1)) # Reset layout


# 4. Plot the log-transformed variables against avg_reviews for comparison
png("plots/scatterplots_log_transformed.png", width = 1600, height = 1200, res = 180)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))

plot(books_clean$log_price, books_clean$avg_reviews,
     xlab = "Log(Price + 1)", ylab = "Avg Reviews",
     main = "Log Price vs Avg Reviews", col = "darkblue", pch = 16, cex = 0.6)

plot(books_clean$log_pages, books_clean$avg_reviews,
     xlab = "Log(Pages + 1)", ylab = "Avg Reviews",
     main = "Log Pages vs Avg Reviews", col = "darkblue", pch = 16, cex = 0.6)

plot(books_clean$log_n_reviews, books_clean$avg_reviews,
```

# 5. Hypothesis testing

## Hypothesis 1: Price vs page count

- **H0:** no correlation between `pages` and `log(1 + price)`.
- **H1:** page count is significantly correlated with log price.


```{r hypothesis-1}
# --- Hypothesis 1: Price vs Page Count (OLS vs. LOESS vs. Nadaraya-Watson) ---

# 1. Perform Pearson correlation test to evaluate linear association
cor_test_h1 <- cor.test(books_clean$pages, log(1 + books_clean$price), method = "pearson")
print(cor_test_h1)

# Keep only books with both pages and price, so the (x, y) pairs stay matched
cc_h1 <- complete.cases(books_clean$pages, books_clean$price)
nw_fit <- as.data.frame(
  ksmooth(books_clean$pages[cc_h1],
          log1p(books_clean$price[cc_h1]),
          kernel = "normal", bandwidth = 100)
)

# 2. Visualize the models using ggplot2 (handling missing values on-the-fly)
p <- ggplot(books_clean, aes(x = pages, y = log(1 + price))) +
  # Scatterplot representing individual book observations
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, color = "#2c3e50") +
  
  # Linear OLS regression fit (parametric baseline)
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", aes(color = "OLS Linear"), se = FALSE, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  
  # LOESS (Local Polynomial Regression) fit to capture non-linearities
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", aes(color = "LOESS (Local Poly)"), se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  
  # Nadaraya-Watson Kernel Regression estimator (local constant smoothing)
  geom_line(
    data = nw_fit,
    aes(x = x, y = y, color = "Nadaraya-Watson"),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  
  # Define custom colors for each estimation method
  scale_color_manual(
    name = "Estimation Method",
    values = c("OLS Linear" = "red", "LOESS (Local Poly)" = "blue", "Nadaraya-Watson" = "darkgreen")
  ) +
  
  # Add titles, axis labels, and statistical context
  labs(
    title = "Hypothesis 1: Price vs. Page Count",
    subtitle = "Comparison of Parametric (OLS) and Non-Parametric (LOESS & Nadaraya-Watson) Estimators",
    x = "Page Count (pages)",
    y = "Log Price (log(1 + price))"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# 3. Save plot using ggsave
file_path <- file.path(plots_dir, "hypothesis_1_price_pages.png")

ggsave(
  filename = file_path,
  plot = p,
  width = 10,
  height = 7,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 150
)
```

**Result.** Pearson's test gives a significant positive correlation between pages and log price (r = 0.49, p < 2.2e-16), so H0 is rejected. Up to about 800 pages the OLS line and the LOESS curve agree. Above 1,000 pages the data are sparse, so the Nadaraya-Watson curve fluctuates there.

## Hypothesis 2: Price by review status

- **H0:** mean log price is the same for books with and without reviews.
- **H1:** the means differ.

```{r hypothesis-2}
# --- Hypothesis 2: Price Differentiation by Review Engagement ---

# 1. Create a binary engagement variable based on review counts
books_clean$has_reviews <- factor(
  ifelse(!is.na(books_clean$n_reviews) & books_clean$n_reviews > 0, "With Reviews", "No Reviews")
)

# 2. Perform Welch Two-Sample t-test
t_test_h2 <- t.test(log(1 + price) ~ has_reviews, data = books_clean)
print(t_test_h2)

# 3. Visualize the price distribution across review status (Boxplot & Violin plot)
p <- ggplot(books_clean, aes(x = has_reviews, y = log(1 + price), fill = has_reviews)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.3, trim = FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.2, outlier.color = "red", alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("No Reviews" = "#e74c3c", "With Reviews" = "#2ecc71")) +
  labs(
    title = "Hypothesis 2: Price Comparison by Review Status",
    subtitle = "Welch Two-Sample t-Test on Log-Transformed Prices",
    x = "Review Engagement Status",
    y = "Log Price (log(1 + price))"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# 4. Save the plot using ggsave
file_path <- file.path(plots_dir, "hypothesis_2_price_reviews.png")

ggsave(
  filename = file_path,
  plot = p,
  width = 10,
  height = 7,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 150
)

```

**Result.** Welch's t-test shows a significant difference (t = 2.72, p = 0.007). Books without reviews have a higher mean log price (3.94 vs 3.78).

## Hypothesis 3: Ratings by review engagement

- **H0:** average rating is the same for high- and low-engagement books (split at the median review count).
- **H1:** average ratings differ between the two groups.

```{r hypothesis-3}
# Hypothesis 3: Ratings Variation Across Review Engagement Levels 
# Note: Since avg_reviews is structurally NA for books with zero reviews, 
# we evaluate rating variation within the subset of reviewed books based on review volume (median split).

# 1. Filter for books with reviews and valid average ratings
reviewed_books <- subset(books_clean, !is.na(avg_reviews) & n_reviews > 0)

# 2. Create binary engagement groups (High vs. Low based on median review count)
median_reviews <- median(reviewed_books$n_reviews, na.rm = TRUE)
reviewed_books$engagement_group <- factor(
  ifelse(reviewed_books$n_reviews >= median_reviews, "High Engagement", "Low Engagement")
)

# 3. Parametric Two-Sample Welch t-test
t_test_h3_alt <- t.test(avg_reviews ~ engagement_group, data = reviewed_books)
print(t_test_h3_alt)

# 4. Non-parametric Wilcoxon rank-sum test (Mann-Whitney U)
wilcox_h3_alt <- wilcox.test(avg_reviews ~ engagement_group, data = reviewed_books)
print(wilcox_h3_alt)

# 5. Boxplot & Violin plot Visualization
p <- ggplot(reviewed_books, aes(x = engagement_group, y = avg_reviews, fill = engagement_group)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.3, trim = FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.2, outlier.color = "red", alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Low Engagement" = "#3498db", "High Engagement" = "#9b59b6")) +
  labs(
    title = "Hypothesis 3: Average Ratings by Review Engagement Level",
    subtitle = "Comparing High vs. Low Review Count Subsamples (Welch t-test & Wilcoxon)",
    x = "Engagement Group (Based on Median Review Count)",
    y = "Average Rating (avg_reviews)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# 6. Save the plot using ggsave
file_path <- file.path(plots_dir, "hypothesis_3_ratings_engagement.png")

ggsave(
  filename = file_path,
  plot = p,
  width = 10,
  height = 7,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 150
)
```

## Hypothesis 4: Review volume vs price

- **H0:** `n_reviews` is not correlated with log price.
- **H1:** the two are correlated.

```{r hypothesis-4}
# --- Hypothesis 4: Review Volume (n_reviews) vs Log Price ---
# 1. Spearman Rank Correlation (robust against heavy tails)
cor_h4 <- cor.test(books_clean$n_reviews, log(1 + books_clean$price), method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
print(cor_h4)

# 2. Scatterplot with Log-Log Scale and LOESS fit
p <- ggplot(books_clean, aes(x = log(1 + n_reviews), y = log(1 + price))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, color = "#2980b9") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red", linetype = "dashed", se = FALSE) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", color = "darkblue", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Hypothesis 4: Log Review Volume vs. Log Price",
    subtitle = "Spearman Correlation & Non-Parametric Fit",
    x = "Log Review Count (log(1 + n_reviews))",
    y = "Log Price (log(1 + price))"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# 3. Save the plot using ggsave
file_path <- file.path(plots_dir, "hypothesis_4_reviews_price.png")

ggsave(
  filename = file_path,
  plot = p,
  width = 10,
  height = 7,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 150
)
```

**Result.** Spearman's test shows a weak negative correlation (rho = -0.16, p = 1.6e-6), so H0 is rejected. Books with more reviews tend to be cheaper.

## Hypothesis 5: Average rating vs price (quality premium)

- **H0:** `avg_reviews` is not correlated with log price.
- **H1:** the two are correlated.

```{r hypothesis-5}
# 1. Spearman Rank Correlation
cor_h5 <- cor.test(books_clean$avg_reviews, log(1 + books_clean$price), method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
print(cor_h5)

# 2. Scatterplot with LOESS fit
p <- ggplot(books_clean, aes(x = avg_reviews, y = log(1 + price))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, color = "#27ae60") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red", linetype = "dashed", se = FALSE) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", color = "darkgreen", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Hypothesis 5: Average Rating vs. Log Price",
    subtitle = "Testing the Quality Premium Hypothesis",
    x = "Average Rating (avg_reviews)",
    y = "Log Price (log(1 + price))"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# 3. Save the plot using ggsave
file_path <- file.path(plots_dir, "hypothesis_5_rating_price.png")

ggsave(
  filename = file_path,
  plot = p,
  width = 10,
  height = 7,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 150
)

```

**Result.** rho = 0.02, p = 0.57, so H0 is not rejected. There is no quality premium.

# 6. Multivariate regression

## 6.1 OLS model for log price

```{r ols-model}
# --- Step 1: Multivariate OLS Model Construction ---
# Model specification based on validated hypotheses (H1, H2, H4)
ols_model <- lm(log(1 + price) ~ pages + has_reviews + log(1 + n_reviews), data = books_clean)

# Summary of the model output
summary_ols <- summary(ols_model)
print(summary_ols)

# --- Step 2: Diagnostic Checks ---

# 1. Multicollinearity check (VIF < 5 indicates no severe multicollinearity)


vif_values <- vif(ols_model)
print("--- Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) ---")
print(vif_values)

# 2. Diagnostic Plots (Residuals vs Fitted, Q-Q Plot, Scale-Location, Residuals vs Leverage)

file_path_diag <- file.path(plots_dir, "ols_model_diagnostics.png")

png(filename = file_path_diag, width = 10, height = 8, units = "in", res = 150)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(ols_model)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
dev.off()
```

**Interpretation.** The model is significant overall (F = 127.6) and the adjusted R² is about 0.29.

- **Pages:** positive effect, about +0.15% in price per extra page.
- **has_reviews:** not significant once `log(1 + n_reviews)` is in the model.
- **log(1 + n_reviews):** negative effect (about -0.072).

All VIF values are below 2, so multicollinearity is not a problem.

## 6.2 Models for average rating

```{r rating-models}
model_formulas <- list(
  "1. Without Stars" = avg_reviews ~ pages + log(1 + price) + log(1 + n_reviews),
  "2. With Star5"    = avg_reviews ~ pages + log(1 + price) + log(1 + n_reviews) + star5,
  "3. With Star5 & Star4" = avg_reviews ~ pages + log(1 + price) + log(1 + n_reviews) + star5 + log(1 + star4)
)

# Loop through each specification to fit the model and check diagnostics
for (model_name in names(model_formulas)) {
  
  # Print separator and current model name
  cat("==================================================\n")
  cat("Model Specification:", model_name, "\n")
  cat("==================================================\n")
  
  # Fit the OLS regression model
  current_model <- lm(model_formulas[[model_name]], data = books_clean)
  
  # Print the regression summary output
  print(summary(current_model))
  
  # Calculate and print Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) for multicollinearity check
  cat("\n--- Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) ---\n")
  print(car::vif(current_model))
  
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

## 6.3 VIF chart

```{r vif-chart}
# 1. Calculate VIF values from your fitted OLS model
vif_vals <- vif(ols_model)

# 2. Convert the VIF vector into a clean data frame for ggplot
vif_df <- data.frame(
  Variable = names(vif_vals),
  VIF = as.numeric(vif_vals)
)

# 3. Create the VIF bar chart using ggplot2
p_vif <- ggplot(vif_df, aes(x = reorder(Variable, VIF), y = VIF, fill = VIF)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, alpha = 0.8, color = "black") +
  # Add a horizontal dashed line representing the critical threshold (e.g., 5.0)
  geom_hline(yintercept = 5.0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  coord_flip() + # Makes it a horizontal bar chart for clean label reading
  labs(
    title = "Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) Diagnostics",
    subtitle = "Checking for Multicollinearity (Threshold = 5.0)",
    x = "Predictor Variables",
    y = "VIF Value"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14)
  )

# 4. Save the plot to your specified directory
file_path_vif <- file.path(plots_dir, "vif_diagnostics_chart.png")
ggsave(filename = file_path_vif, plot = p_vif, width = 8, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 150)
```

# 7. Conclusions

- **Page count is the main driver of price.**
- **Books with more reviews tend to be cheaper.** This points to a mass-market discounting effect.
- **Higher ratings do not come with higher prices.** There is no quality premium.
- **Language was dropped.** Almost all books are in English.
